summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), help children represent addition and subtraction using objects, drawings, fingers, mental images, spoken language, and number sentences — and, crucially, move fluidly between these so they see that they all show the SAME calculation. Deliberately cycle one calculation through multiple representations and link them explicitly ('show me where the 2 is in your drawing'), progressing from concrete toward mental imagery so efficient strategies can replace counting-all.
misconceptions: Treating each representation as a separate, unrelated task and not seeing that the objects, drawing and number sentence all show the SAME calculation.
Drawing elaborate pictures that obscure quantity (detailed apples instead of countable dots), losing the mathematical point.
Staying dependent on concrete objects and not progressing toward drawings/mental images, so efficiency never develops.
Mis-mapping between representations — e.g. drawing the total when the story described only one part.
Using a drawing as decoration after getting an answer another way, rather than as a tool to find or explain the answer.

activities.title: Linked windows onto one calculation
steps: Place counters onto a mat to show a given sum such as 3 + 2.
Watch linked representations update together: a ten-frame fills, a dot-drawing sketches itself, and the number sentence 3 + 2 = 5 assembles alongside the counters.
Tap the '2' in the number sentence and see exactly two counters, two dots, and two ten-frame cells light up at once across every pane.
Try a 'cover a window' challenge: predict what the drawing will look like before it is revealed, then check.
activities.insight: The objects, drawing, ten-frame and number sentence are not separate exercises — they are the same quantity shown different ways; and I can begin to carry the picture in my head.

activities.title: Show it with cubes, then with a drawing
steps: Use cubes or counters to show a spoken addition, e.g. build 3 and 2 pushed together to make 5.
Draw a picture (dots or marks) that matches the same calculation.
Narrate aloud what you did, e.g. 'I drew 3 dots and 2 more dots, and that makes 5.'
Point to the '3' and the '2' in the cubes, then point to them in your drawing.
activities.insight: I can represent the same calculation two different ways and show how they correspond, using quick countable marks rather than detailed pictures.

activities.title: Enact subtraction as taking away
steps: Start with 5 cubes and show 5 − 1 by actually removing one cube, leaving four.
Say the number sentence aloud: '5 take away 1 leaves 4, so 5 − 1 = 4.'
Explain which cube you took away and how many are left.
Contrast this with 4 + 1: show how combining to make 5 is different from taking away to leave 4.
activities.insight: One way subtraction works is taking away: starting with an amount and removing part of it. That is different from putting two groups together.

activities.title: Match and talk about representations (supporting activities)
steps: Match a drawing to the number sentence that shows the same calculation.
Respond to the prompt 'Show me another way to draw that' and produce a second representation.
Use structured models consistently — ten-frames, five-frames, or a part-part-whole ('cherry') diagram — so representations accumulate meaning.
activities.insight: The same calculation can be recognised across formats, and structured models give it a consistent, reusable shape.

checkQuestion: Here are 3 cubes and 2 more cubes pushed together (show them). What number sentence does this show? Now YOU show me 5 − 1 using the cubes.
checkAnswer: Reads the cubes as 3 + 2 = 5 (combining); then models 5 − 1 by starting with five cubes and taking one away, leaving four, and can say 5 − 1 = 4.
